/about-us.title: About us | AURÉLION
/about-us.description: A hotel run by the people who chose it. Our history, our house, and the family behind it since 1923.
h3: A hotel is only as good as the people who keep it.
h5: One hundred years of quiet magnificence.
p: Aurélion has always been a house run by individuals who chose it deliberately. Not a posting, not a stepping stone — but a place they came to and decided to stay. The head sommelier has spent nineteen years curating Le Cellier. The head housekeeper knows the preferred pillow firmness of guests who have not visited in three years. The night porter has watched the lake in every season and will tell you, without hesitation, that November is the finest month.

This continuity is not accidental. It is the result of a culture that values discretion over display, craft over spectacle, and the long relationship over the single impression. Staff at Aurélion are not trained to follow a script. They are trusted to understand what a guest needs before it is asked.

At the head of the house is General Manager Thomas Beaumont — the third generation of the family that built Aurélion in 1923. He arrived in 2006 after several years abroad and has not left since. His presence in the hotel is quiet and constant. He is as likely to be found in conversation with the kitchen brigade at six in the morning as greeting a long-standing guest in the lobby at midnight. Under his stewardship, Aurélion has remained precisely what his grandfather intended — a place of unhurried refinement, where the standard is set not by industry benchmarks, but by the expectations of the guests who return, year after year, to the same room, the same table, the same view.

On the fourteenth of September 2023, Aurélion marks one hundred years. No grand celebration. No press event. Only a letter, sent to every guest who had ever stayed, with a single line: "The lake is still here. So are we."

The Beaumont family undertakes the most comprehensive restoration in the hotel's history. Every room is dismantled and rebuilt. Nothing is added that cannot justify its presence. The result is not a renovation — it is a refinement.

Chef Antoine Marchand joins Aurélion and redefines the hotel's culinary identity. His insistence on Alpine produce and seasonal menus — radical at the time — establishes a kitchen philosophy that remains unchanged fifty years later.

Drawing from the thermal waters of Lac Léman, the Lumière Spa opens on the lower ground floor. It is the first hotel spa in the region to offer treatments rooted in Alpine botanicals and Swiss hydrotherapy.

The hotel's most significant expansion — a new wing of twenty rooms, each facing the lake, each with floor-to-ceiling windows. The Lakeview Suite is introduced for the first time. It remains the most requested room in the house to this day.

Head sommelier Georges Vernet begins assembling what will become Le Cellier — a private collection of Burgundy and Rhône Valley vintages that today numbers over 1,200 labels. The first bottle opened from the original collection remains on display in the wine room.

By the early 1930s, Aurélion has become one of the most discreetly sought-after addresses in Europe. Writers, diplomats and composers find in it something grander establishments cannot offer — the particular luxury of being left alone.

Swiss hotelier Henri Beaumont opens Aurélion on the fourteenth of September with thirty-two rooms, a single dining room and an unwritten promise: that every guest would leave better than they arrived.

/wellness-spa.title: Wellness & Spa | AURÉLION
/wellness-spa.description: Alpine wellness, refined. Thermal waters of Lac Léman and the botanicals of the surrounding meadows.
h2: Not a spa you visit. A ritual you carry with you.
h5: Where the water of Lac Léman meets the botanicals of the Alps.
p: Lumière Spa draws from two sources that have defined this landscape for centuries — the thermal waters of Lac Léman and the botanicals of the surrounding alpine meadows. Pine, juniper, wild thyme, glacial mineral water. Ingredients that predate the hotel by a thousand years, and treatments that have been refined over the course of a century to make the most of them.

Carved from pale travertine and fed by the thermal waters of Lac Léman, the Lumière indoor pool is the still centre of the spa. Thirty metres of uninterrupted water, lit by narrow skylights that track the movement of the day. There is no music. There is no rush. There is only the water.

Six fully private treatment rooms, each designed around silence and natural material — stone, linen, aged oak. Every room is temperature-controlled, naturally lit where possible, and prepared individually for each guest before arrival. No two treatments are identical. No two guests are treated the same way.

A traditional hammam and a separate eucalyptus steam room, available to all spa guests without reservation. The hammam is heated to 45°C and dressed in hand-laid mosaic tile. The steam room draws from a blend of Swiss alpine botanicals — pine, juniper and wild thyme. Both rooms open at seven and close with the day.

A quietly equipped fitness space overlooking the private garden — free weights, resistance machines, cardio equipment and a dedicated stretching area. Personal training sessions are available on request, as are guided morning runs along the lakeside path. Open to hotel guests at all hours.
Open 24h for hotel guests | Personal training on request

The room where a treatment is allowed to finish properly. Eight daybeds dressed in heavy linen, low light, and tall windows that give the lake back to you without asking anything in return. Alpine herbal infusions and cold spring water are set out through the day. Conversation is neither forbidden nor encouraged.
Complimentary for spa guests | No reservation required

On the lower terrace, sheltered from the wind by a stone wall and an espaliered hedge, the outdoor hot tub offers something the indoor spaces cannot — the cold of the alpine air against the heat of the water. Available year-round. At its finest in winter, when the lake fogs and the mountains disappear.
